question.prompt: For each positive integer \(n,\) let \(f_1(n)\) be twice the number of positive integer divisors of \(n,\) and for \(j \ge 2,\) let \(f_j(n) = f_1(f_{j-1}(n)).\) For how many values of \(n \le 50\) is \(f_{50}(n) = 12?\)

solutions.title: Follow divisor counts by prime pattern
solutions.explanation:
The useful observation is that repeated divisor counting quickly reaches a value that stops changing. Write \(F(n)=f_1(n)\). In particular,
\[
F(8)=2(4)=8,\qquad F(12)=2(6)=12.
\]
Once an iterate reaches either value, every later iterate stays there.

If \(n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}\), a divisor independently chooses an exponent from \(0\) through \(a_i\) for each prime. Thus
\[
F(n)=2(a_1+1)\cdots(a_k+1).
\]
We can therefore classify inputs by their prime exponents. Below, \(p,q,r\) denote distinct primes, and each arrow means another application of \(F\).

| Form of \(n\) | Successive values under \(F\) |
| --- | --- |
| \(1\) | \(2\to4\to6\to8\) |
| \(p\) | \(4\to6\to8\) |
| \(p^2\) | \(6\to8\) |
| \(p^3\) | \(8\) |
| \(p^4\) | \(10\to8\) |
| \(p^5\) | \(12\) |
| \(pq\) | \(8\) |
| \(p^2q\) | \(12\) |
| \(p^3q\) | \(16\to10\to8\) |
| \(p^4q\) | \(20\to12\) |
| \(p^2q^2\) | \(18\to12\) |
| \(pqr\) | \(16\to10\to8\) |

These forms cover every positive integer at most \(50\):

- With one distinct prime, the exponent is at most \(5\), since \(2^6=64>50\).
- With two distinct primes, an exponent of at least \(5\) would give at least \(2^5\cdot3=96\). Exponents at least \(3\) and \(2\) would give at least \(2^3\cdot3^2=72\). This leaves exactly the five two-prime forms in the table.
- With three distinct primes, increasing any exponent above \(1\) gives at least \(2^2\cdot3\cdot5=60\).
- Four distinct primes give at least \(2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210\).

Every row reaches \(8\) or \(12\) within four applications, so the fiftieth iterate is \(12\) exactly for the forms \(p^2q,p^5,p^2q^2,p^4q\). Count them as follows:

- For \(p^2q\), the squared prime can only be \(2,3,5\), since \(7^2\cdot2>50\). Taking \(p=2\) gives \(12,20,28,44\); taking \(p=3\) gives \(18,45\); taking \(p=5\) gives \(50\). There are \(7\) numbers.
- For \(p^5\), only \(2^5=32\) fits, since \(3^5>50\).
- For \(p^2q^2=(pq)^2\), only \(pq=2\cdot3\) fits: the next possible distinct-prime product is \(2\cdot5=10\), whose square exceeds \(50\). This gives \(36\).
- For \(p^4q\), \(p\) must be \(2\), since \(3^4\cdot2>50\). Then \(q\le50/16\) and \(q\ne2\), so \(q=3\), giving \(48\).

Unique prime factorization ensures that these four forms do not overlap. The requested count is
\[
7+1+1+1=\boxed{10},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
